nature-clim-127.title: The price of oil: one number the world watches
nature-clim-127.text: In July 2008 oil peaked at US$147 a barrel. By December it had fallen to US$34 as the financial crisis took hold. The price of oil is the spot price of a barrel of benchmark crude, such as Brent or West Texas Intermediate. Buyers and sellers use it as a reference. It is set by global supply and demand rather than any one country's output, though the OPEC cartel pushes prices up. Prices were fairly steady from 1861 until the 1970s, when the 1973 and 1979 crises drove a significant rise. The main drivers have been shocks to supply, demand, storage and global growth. In 2014, after a supply glut, prices began a 70% drop lasting to 2016, one of the three biggest declines since World War II. High prices generally hurt growth and raise the cost of many products, including food. Costs differ widely: in 2019 Middle Eastern oil broke even at about US$42 a barrel and oil sands at US$83.

nature-clim-174.title: Just transition: leaving no one behind
nature-clim-174.text: In the 1980s, US trade unions sought protection for workers hit by environmental rules. Tony Mazzocchi of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union proposed a 'Superfund for Workers' to compensate and retrain them. He is believed to have coined the term just transition. The principle holds that the shift to a low-carbon economy should treat people fairly and leave no workers, places or countries behind. Unions won just transition and decent work language in the preamble of the 2015 Paris climate deal. The IPCC stresses low-emission industries, fair jobs, equitable energy access and economic diversification. As of 2022, 38% of 170 countries mentioned it in their short-term climate plans. The EU's Just Transition mechanism helps regions dependent on fossil fuels move to a greener economy.

nature-clim-176.title: Climate policy and stranded fossil assets
nature-clim-176.text: For a 50 percent chance of 1.5°C, a 2021 study found, nearly 60 percent of oil and gas reserves must stay unused. So must 90 percent of coal reserves. Those reserves would lose their value. Climate-related asset stranding is this loss of value for fossil fuel reserves and carbon-intensive plants as policy, technology and markets shift. It hits oil, gas and coal companies, industries such as steel, aluminium and cement, and fossil-exporting countries and workers. Risk factors include environmental change, carbon pricing, falling clean-tech costs, changing social norms and litigation. A 2026 estimate found early closure of coal plants for a 1.5°C pathway would strand around $842 billion. Fossil fuel importers gain from switching, while exporters face the losses.

nature-clim-270.title: Carbon accounting: keeping the books on emissions
nature-clim-270.text: No one can cut what they cannot count. Carbon accounting is a set of methods for measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organization emits. Organizations use it to set a baseline, choose reduction targets and track progress. It works at every scale, from companies and cities up to national greenhouse gas inventories. Standards such as {{ref:nature-gov-109}} and ISO 14064 sort emissions into three scopes. Scope 1 covers direct emissions, Scope 2 purchased energy, and Scope 3 the wider value chain. Scope 3 is often the largest share of a company's emissions and the hardest to report accurately. Accurate counts matter beyond the firm. Carbon credit markets depend on them, and investors use them to judge a company's climate risks. There is some evidence that programs requiring this accounting help lower emissions.

nature-clim-268.title: The Stern Review: the greatest market failure
nature-clim-268.text: On 30 October 2006, the economist Stern, profiled in {{ref:nature-hist-045}}, released a 700-page review of the economics of climate change for the UK government. It called climate change the greatest and widest-ranging market failure ever seen. Its main conclusion was that the benefits of strong, early action far outweigh the costs of not acting. Without action, it estimated losses of at least 5% of global GDP each year, possibly 20% or more counting wider risks. It proposed investing 1% of global GDP a year. In 2008 Stern raised that to 2%, saying the Review had underestimated the risks and that warming was faster than expected. The most debated point was its near-zero pure rate of time preference, which counts future welfare almost as much as today's. Stern held it to be the only ethical choice. Some economists called the Review deeply flawed, while others, including Kenneth Arrow, judged its main conclusion justified. The disputes over its discount rate, damages and costs continue.

nature-clim-252.title: Climate scenarios: plausible stories about the future
nature-clim-252.text: Nobody can forecast the far future, but analysts can sketch the possibilities. A climate change scenario is a plausible picture of how the future might unfold, built on assumptions about the main forces driving climate change. Three key inputs are population, economic activity and new technology. Scenarios help test how well mitigation and adaptation will work over the long term. A baseline scenario is the reference case, against which an alternative such as a mitigation scenario is compared. Pathways are related but more concrete: a roadmap of the actions needed to make a scenario come true. One finding cuts against intuition. Economic growth has proved compatible with both rising and falling emissions, depending on efficiency, energy sources and the shift toward services. Countries use scenarios when drawing up adaptation plans and the climate pledges each country makes.

nature-clim-248.title: Integrated assessment models: the economy and the sky in one framework
nature-clim-248.text: Climate policy needs a tool that links factories to the atmosphere. Integrated assessment modelling tries to provide one, joining the main features of society and the economy with the biosphere and atmosphere in a single framework. Its goal is to inform policy-making, usually on climate change. Every climate integrated assessment model (IAM) includes economic processes and the processes that produce greenhouse gases. These models do not predict the future. Instead they estimate what possible scenarios look like. They come in two broad families. Process-based models map detailed pathways. Aggregate models add up the total costs of climate change and of mitigation. Cost-benefit IAMs such as DICE, PAGE and FUND are the main tools for estimating the social cost of carbon. The models have been severely criticized. Critics say they create an illusory sense of precision and handle justice poorly. They have also been accused of undervaluing wind and solar power while overvaluing bioenergy and carbon capture. Because the models exist to inform policy, such biases matter. Their treatment of uncertainty remains disputed as well.

nature-clim-223.title: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three roots of climate risk
nature-clim-223.text: Global disaster losses have grown mainly because more people and wealth are exposed, though human-caused climate change also plays a part. The IPCC captures this in a framework where climate risk arises from three interacting factors. A hazard is the climate event itself. Exposure is who and what lies in its path. The third factor, described in {{ref:nature-clim-025}}, measures how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed, formally their propensity to be adversely affected. Each factor may be uncertain in both size and likelihood. Because risk comes from their interaction, adaptation can lower it by acting on all three.

nature-clim-247.title: DICE: Nordhaus's model of climate and the economy
nature-clim-247.text: In a 1992 Cowles Foundation discussion paper, the economist Nordhaus, profiled in {{ref:nature-hist-050}}, proposed the DICE model. It combines economics, the carbon cycle, climate science and impacts to weigh the costs and benefits of slowing climate change. A regional variant, RICE, followed in 1996. Its central assumption is that externalities create costs missing from prices, which government must add. It discounts the future at the market return on capital, around 4% on average. The US Environmental Protection Agency uses it as one of three main models for the social cost of carbon. Its answers have shifted. In 2020, a rerun with updated science and discount rates put the optimal goal below 2.0 °C of warming, not the 3.5 °C Nordhaus first found. A 2020 paper with an updated damage function found around 2 °C optimal, depending on climate sensitivity. DICE treats innovation as external. A variant with induced technical change favors strong early investment in mitigation. Critics attack its sensitivity to assumptions and its discount rate.

nature-clim-265.title: The Kaya identity: four levers behind every ton of CO2
nature-clim-265.text: Total carbon dioxide emissions can be written as four numbers multiplied together. The Kaya identity, developed by the Japanese energy economist Yoichi Kaya, uses population, GDP per person, energy used per unit of GDP, and emissions per unit of energy. In theory the factors cancel out. The point is practical: the identity lets emissions be estimated from readily available data. It is a form of Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren's equation for environmental impact, described in {{ref:nature-eecon-183}}. It also shows the levers for cutting emissions, notably energy per unit of GDP and emissions per unit of energy. It plays a core role in building future emissions scenarios in the IPCC Special Report on Emissions Scenarios. Energy used per unit of GDP has generally declined worldwide, through efficiency, technology and shifts in economic structure.

nature-clim-251.title: Carbon lock-in: why fossil systems are hard to leave
nature-clim-251.text: Low-carbon technologies that are already cost-effective often spread slowly, a puzzle called the climate policy paradox. Carbon lock-in helps explain it. Gregory Unruh coined the term in a 1999 doctoral thesis for the self-reinforcing inertia of large fossil-fuel energy systems. Technology networks grow together with the institutions and habits that benefit from them, fed by increasing returns to scale. The result is a form of the pattern described in {{ref:nature-pol-038}}. Car-based transport and fossil-fuel power systems are examples. A 2007 report sorted the barriers into three kinds: cost-effectiveness, financial and legal, and intellectual property. The risk is current. Building new natural gas infrastructure threatens fresh lock-in and investments that lose their value early, the subject of {{ref:nature-clim-175}}.

nature-clim-250.title: The carbon bubble: fossil fuel wealth that cannot be burned
nature-clim-250.text: In 2011 the Carbon Tracker Initiative found that the world could burn only 20% of its fossil fuel reserves to stay below 2 °C. The rest would become assets that lose their value early, explained in {{ref:nature-clim-175}}, though investors treated them as low-risk. Carbon Tracker coined the term carbon bubble, in reports from 2011 and 2013, for the suspected overvaluation that results. The limit behind it is the upper limit on CO2 emissions that keeps warming below a given level, explored in {{ref:nature-clim-136}}. A 2021 analysis tightened the squeeze. For even a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C, 90% of coal and 60% of oil and gas reserves could not be extracted. Quarterly results and accounting standards push investors to ignore such long-term risks. An orderly transition away from fossil fuels could prevent a disruptive bursting of the bubble.

nature-clim-235.title: Cost-effectiveness: the cheapest route to a set goal
nature-clim-235.text: When benefits are hard to price, analysts can skip that step. Cost-effectiveness analysis in climate policy ranks options by their cost per unit of a set goal. For mitigation the goal is usually tonnes of greenhouse gas cut, giving a cost such as dollars per tonne of CO2. Adaptation has no common goal, so the measure might be hectares of land at risk from rising seas. The method can find the cheapest way to meet a fixed target, such as a sector's emissions cut.

nature-clim-272.title: FUND: Richard Tol's region-by-region model
nature-clim-272.text: FUND, Richard Tol's integrated assessment model, estimates climate damages region by region and sector by sector. It covers impacts such as agriculture, health and rising seas, and includes some adaptation over time. Unusually, it allows negative damages, meaning some regions or sectors gain from warming. Its assumptions about adaptation and warming benefits can understate damages. It is used for the social cost of carbon, though a reviewer of the Copenhagen Consensus said relying on it alone was not reasonable.

nature-clim-214.title: Termination shock: the danger of stopping
nature-clim-214.text: Solar radiation modification masks warming rather than removing its cause. Stop it suddenly while greenhouse gas levels are high, and the hidden warming would arrive fast. This termination shock would bring rapid temperature rise, rising seas and weaker carbon sinks. Large-scale use would likely need a commitment of decades to a century. The IPCC notes that a gradual phase-out alongside mitigation would reduce the impact.

nature-clim-243.title: DICE, FUND and PAGE: three models, three answers
nature-clim-243.text: For years, three integrated assessment models underpinned estimates of the social cost of carbon. DICE finds a single global optimal path and assumes damages grow with the square of temperature, with no tipping points. FUND estimates impacts by region and sector, and lets some regions gain from warming. PAGE is probabilistic, using Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random trials, of thousands of futures, catastrophes included. Their methods can give dramatically different values, so the Obama-era estimate averaged runs of all three.

nature-clim-249.title: Process-based models: mapping the road sector by sector
nature-clim-249.text: How exactly could the world meet the 1.5 °C goal set by {{ref:nature-clim-074}}? Process-based integrated assessment models map detailed sector-by-sector pathways to such targets, and the IPCC uses them to quantify mitigation scenarios. They underpin energy policy assessment and simulate the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Well-known frameworks include IMAGE, MESSAGEix, AIM/GCE, GCAM, REMIND-MAgPIE and WITCH-GLOBIOM. One pattern recurs: beyond 2050, bioenergy with carbon capture forms a large part of meeting warming goals in their pathways.

nature-clim-258.title: Fat tails: when disaster is likelier than it looks
nature-clim-258.text: The market crashes of 1929, 1987 and 2008 were not mathematically well-behaved events. They show why fat-tailed distributions matter. In such a distribution, extreme outcomes are much more likely than in a normal, bell-shaped, or exponential one. The most extreme case has a tail that decays like a power law. Fitting a normal distribution to fat-tailed data understates the true risk. Weitzman, profiled in {{ref:nature-hist-081}}, argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails, which standard climate economics handles poorly.

nature-clim-108.title: Efficiency: the first fuel
nature-clim-108.text: Between 1974 and 2010, efficiency measures avoided more energy use in the IEA's member states than any single fuel supplied. That is why energy policy increasingly calls efficient energy use the 'first fuel'. It means reducing the energy needed to provide the same products and services. An insulated building, for example, stays comfortable while using less energy for heating and cooling. The two main motives are saving operating costs and cutting greenhouse gas emissions, and it can also reduce dependence on imported energy. Efficient technology usually carries an upfront capital cost, and life-cycle assessment can compare the costs over time. The potential is large. Better efficiency in buildings, industry and transport could cut the world's energy needs in 2050 by one third. The IEA estimates it could deliver 40% of the emission cuts the Paris goals need. Its extra benefits, such as cleaner air, better health and more secure supplies, have sometimes been valued above the energy savings themselves. California shows what policy can do. Its efficiency standards from the mid-1970s kept per-capita energy use about flat while US consumption doubled. Tools include carbon taxes, efficiency standards for appliances, buildings and vehicles, and subsidies for efficient equipment.

nature-clim-133.title: Energy economics: how societies supply and use power
nature-clim-133.text: In 1865 W.S. Jevons worried that Britain would run short of coal. Energy has been prominent in economics since the 1973 oil crisis, but the worry is old. Energy economics studies how societies supply and use energy, and the costs and value of energy services. Those services are the end uses energy provides, such as lighting, heating and fuel, and the aim is to deliver them with the least energy input. It is an applied branch of economics, drawing on engineering, geology, political science and ecology rather than standing alone. Its topics include how strongly supply and demand respond to price in energy markets, and the liberalization and regulation of electricity markets. Hotelling's rule gave an early price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels. Its theory has grown around three themes: the way efficiency saves less than expected, the energy efficiency gap and, more recently, gentle pushes toward greener choices. Vaclav Smil goes further. He argues that every economic activity is at root a conversion of energy, with money only a rough proxy for valuing energy flows.

nature-clim-114.title: Energy security: when supply becomes a matter of state
nature-clim-114.text: Modern economies run on affordable energy, and supplies are spread unevenly among countries. That creates serious vulnerabilities, which is why energy security links a nation's security to the reliable availability of energy. Threats include instability in producing countries, supply manipulation, and attacks on pipelines and grids. The 1973 oil crisis and the rise of the OPEC cartel pushed countries such as Japan to diversify into gas, nuclear power, mass transit and conservation. Imported natural gas carries sharper short-term risks than oil, as the Russia–Ukraine gas disputes of 2006 and 2009 showed. Wind, solar and efficiency are spread across many countries, unlike fossil fuels. Deploying them and diversifying sources therefore raises security. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine made energy security a stronger driver of Europe's shift away from fossil fuels. Carefully phasing out fossil fuel subsidies would also help, according to the International Institute for Sustainable Development.

nature-clim-170.title: Critical minerals for the energy transition
nature-clim-170.text: The IEA lists 37 critical minerals for clean energy technologies, and expects demand for them to rise 235 per cent by 2050. For mineral-rich countries of Sub-Saharan Africa, that boom may drive the lasting progress described in {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. It has a cost. Mining for these minerals can threaten conservation areas, and in 2023 it contributed strongly to deforestation.

nature-clim-109.title: Rebound: why efficiency saves less than expected
nature-clim-109.text: A fuel-efficient car makes driving cheaper, so its owner may drive farther and give back part of the savings. Economists call this a rebound, a general idea explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-159}}. Efficiency gains make energy services cheaper, so people use more of them. Estimates range from roughly 5% to 40%, likely under 30% for households and nearer 10% for transport. A 30% rebound means an efficiency gain delivers only 70% of the savings engineering models predict. The long view is sobering. Historical analysis shows efficiency gains were almost always outpaced by economic growth, so total resource use and pollution still rose.

nature-clim-112.title: Energy poverty: life without modern energy
nature-clim-112.text: In 2024 an estimated 655 million people had no electricity, and about two billion cooked with polluting fuels and technologies. Energy poverty is this lack of modern energy services, such as electricity and cooking fuel that does not pollute, at home. Causes include missing power plants, lines and pipelines, and prices poorer households cannot afford. It harms health, education and women's opportunities. Household air pollution caused about 2.9 million deaths in 2021, by the WHO's estimate. Women and children in homes burning wood, charcoal or dung do most of the cooking and fuel collection, so they bear most of the harm. Ninety percent of children in Sub-Saharan Africa attend primary schools without electricity. In the Global North it is usually called fuel poverty: homes that cannot afford heating, cooling and power. No single measure is accepted internationally. Clean cook stoves running on LPG or electricity are a recommended low-cost remedy.

nature-clim-117.title: The experience curve: cheaper with every doubling
nature-clim-117.text: In 1936 the engineer Theodore Paul Wright noticed that each doubling of total aircraft production cut the labor needed for a new plane by 20%. The pattern, later put into a formula in {{ref:nature-clim-118}}, is the experience curve effect: costs fall by a steady share each time cumulative production doubles. Other industries show cuts from a couple of percent up to 30% per doubling, usually constant within each industry. Bruce Henderson of the Boston Consulting Group coined the term in the 1960s. Causes include growing worker skill, standardization, specialization, new technology, fuller use of equipment and redesign. Firms therefore gain by expanding early, winning lower costs and larger market share. Storage shows the effect: lithium-ion battery prices fall 19% with each doubling of capacity, while pumped hydro has barely fallen. Critics note the effect is tangled with economies of scale.

nature-clim-151.title: Energy conservation: simply using less
nature-clim-151.text: Heating a room less, driving less and air-drying clothes save energy without any gain in efficiency. Energy conservation means actively using less energy, through changes in behavior as well as better technology. The line between conservation and efficiency can be fuzzy, but both matter environmentally and economically. Conservation sits at the top of the hierarchy of priorities used in {{ref:nature-clim-215}}. There is plenty to save: burning fossil fuels for transport and electricity is less than 50% efficient, with much heat wasted.

nature-clim-149.title: Climate change mitigation: cutting the cause
nature-clim-149.text: To hold warming to 1.5 °C, 2022 assessments said, global emissions must peak before 2025 and fall about 43% by 2030. Climate change mitigation is action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change. It is also called decarbonization. The IPCC defines it as a human intervention to reduce emissions or enhance the sinks of greenhouse gases. The main actions are saving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy. Changing land use and removing CO2 are secondary strategies. Measures fall into four types: clean energy and transport, energy conservation, sustainable agriculture and green industry, and enhancing sinks and carbon removal. Solar and wind can replace fossil fuels at the lowest cost of the renewable options. Some processes resist, and air travel and cement production are among the hardest to decarbonize. The gap remains wide. Adopted policies would still lead to about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100, well above the goal of {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. Mitigation is often seen as a burden to share. It can also be an opportunity for industrial development and exports.

nature-clim-202.title: Greenhouse gas inventories: national emission ledgers
nature-clim-202.text: Almost every country has joined {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, which requires regular inventories of the emissions produced on its territory. A greenhouse gas inventory records the greenhouse gases emitted, and removed by carbon sinks, in a country, region or organization. Counting removals sets it apart from other air emission inventories. Parties to the UN climate convention and to {{ref:nature-clim-056}} must submit annual inventories of human emissions and removals. The simplest method multiplies an amount of activity, such as fuel burned, by an 'emission factor'. Scientists feed inventories into atmospheric models, and policy makers use them to design and track emission cuts.

nature-clim-137.title: Splitting the world's carbon budget
nature-clim-137.text: If the world can emit only so much more CO2, which country gets how much? Dividing the carbon budget requires value judgments about fairness. Nations differ in population, industrialization, past emissions and ability to cut, so scientists apply principles of equity. Under the principle described in {{ref:nature-clim-084}}, countries that emitted more in the past or are richer get smaller budgets. The egalitarian principle shares budgets by population. That raises an awkward question: do individuals have a right to pollute? Grandfathering shares budgets according to each nation's emissions in a base year. It was used under {{ref:nature-clim-056}} and the early EU emissions trading system, and it favors developed countries. Recent work argues that grandfathering is not a standard of equity at all, because it builds in biases against poorer states. Scholars still disagree about which principle should divide the budget.

nature-clim-162.title: Net zero: balancing what goes up with what comes down
nature-clim-162.text: As of November 2023, about 145 countries had announced or were considering net zero targets, covering close to 90% of global emissions. Net-zero emissions is the state in which greenhouse gases released by human activity are balanced by human removals. The idea grew from late-2000s research showing that warming slows only when CO2 emissions reach net zero. It underlies {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. Reaching it is needed to slow warming, though gases already in the air keep causing some. Net zero is not a license to offset. It needs deep emission cuts first, and only a small remaining share can be balanced by taking CO2 back out of the air. Net zero standards require cutting emissions by more than 90% and offsetting only the remaining 10% or less. The economics look favorable. The IMF estimates that net zero by 2050 would leave global GDP 7 percent higher than current policies. Net zero, carbon neutrality and climate neutrality are often used as synonyms, though some standards give them different meanings.

nature-clim-215.title: Sustainable energy: meeting needs without borrowing from the future
nature-clim-215.text: Fossil fuels provide 85% of world energy use, and the energy system causes 76% of greenhouse gas emissions. Sustainable energy is energy that meets present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs. It is judged by its effects on environment, economy and society. Those effects range from greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution to energy poverty and toxic waste. Around 790 million people still lack electricity, and 2.6 billion cook with polluting fuels such as wood or charcoal. Renewables such as wind, hydro, solar and geothermal can harm the environment, but they are generally far more sustainable than fossil fuels. Whether non-renewables belong is disputed. Nuclear avoids carbon and air pollution but brings waste, proliferation and accident risks. Efficiency matters as much as supply: the IEA says it could deliver 40% of the emission cuts the Paris goals need. The bill is large. The IPCC estimates US$2.4 trillion a year must be invested in energy from 2016 to 2035 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.

nature-clim-143.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away
nature-clim-143.text: Using all of Earth's geologic storage would limit warming by only 0.7 °C, a 2025 study found. Storage is no cure-all, yet it is a real tool. Carbon sequestration is the storing of carbon in a carbon pool, a place in the Earth system where carbon stays for a period of time. By lowering the carbon dioxide in the air, it helps manage the carbon cycle and limit climate change. It comes in two main types. Biologic sequestration, or biosequestration, relies on plants, which take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow and bind it into biomass. People can speed this up through land use and farming. But stores such as forests may be temporary, since fires, disease, economic pressure and politics can release the carbon. Geologic sequestration lasts far longer. Injecting CO2 underground, or turning it into carbonate salts, locks carbon away for thousands to millions of years. When carbon is captured and stored, as in {{ref:nature-clim-185}}, sequestration is the storage step.

nature-clim-208.title: The low-carbon economy
nature-clim-208.text: Switching to lower-emission technologies often pays back within 0.5–5 years. A low-carbon economy absorbs as much greenhouse gas as it emits, or more broadly produces far lower emissions. Related terms include carbon-neutral economy and decarbonized economy, with 'carbon' standing for all greenhouse gases. Getting there means cutting emissions in every sector through renewables, efficiency, electric vehicles, heat pumps and climate-smart agriculture. It needs energy policies and incentives such as emissions trading and carbon taxes. Benefits reach ecosystems, trade, jobs, health, energy security and competitiveness. Workers in carbon-intensive industries are more likely to lose jobs, while renewables and building renovation create new ones. The obstacle is a free-rider problem: each country gains from others' mitigation but loses by going low-carbon alone.

nature-clim-185.title: Carbon capture and storage: catching CO2 at the chimney
nature-clim-185.text: As of 2023, carbon capture and storage (CCS) caught about 45 million tonnes of CO2 a year, around 0.1% of global emissions. CCS separates carbon dioxide from industrial sources before it reaches the air and moves it to long-term storage, usually deep underground. Capture usually passes exhaust through an amine solvent that binds CO2. Around 80% of captured CO2 is used for enhanced oil recovery, pumped into oil fields to push out more oil. So CCS is also called carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS). Cost is the sticking point. Capture costs US$15–25 per tonne for concentrated streams such as gas processing. Dilute streams from power, cement and steel plants cost US$40–120. Many other ways to cut emissions cost under US$20 per tonne. Because designs are site-specific, costs fall only slowly as builders gain experience. The research literature gives CCS a small but critical role. Fossil fuel companies, meanwhile, promote it to extend the fossil era. CCS therefore remains politically divisive, with open disagreement over its cost-effectiveness and whether it prolongs fossil fuel use.

nature-clim-178.title: Biochar: charcoal that feeds the soil
nature-clim-178.text: Long before Europeans arrived, Amazonians smoldered farm waste into charcoal, creating soils later settlers called terra preta. Biochar is that kind of charcoal: made by heating biomass with little oxygen, and meant for soil and other organic uses. The process, pyrolysis, yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas. In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions. It helps degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones. Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity. Biochar is so stable that it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies its use for carbon removal, described in {{ref:nature-clim-180}}. A 1–2% share in concrete also cuts emissions from cement.

nature-clim-160.title: Mitigation sector by sector
nature-clim-160.text: Emissions come from every corner of the economy, so cuts are grouped by where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use. Buildings account for 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions. About half their energy goes to heating space and water. Heat pumps are a strong tool there, because a modern one moves about three to five times more heat energy than the electricity it uses. Transport causes 15% of emissions. Public transport, cycling, electric vehicles and rail help cut them. Counting direct and indirect emissions, industry is the largest emitter. Switching to electricity, green hydrogen and measures that keep materials in use can reduce its share. Agriculture and forestry cause almost 20% of emissions, and cattle alone produce 21% of global methane. Each sector therefore needs its own mix of measures.

nature-clim-197.title: Phasing out fossil fuels
nature-clim-197.text: Fossil fuels cause over 70% of greenhouse gas emissions, so phasing them out is the largest part of limiting warming. The proposal is a gradual reduction of their use and production to zero, to cut air pollution, limit climate change and gain energy independence. Policies include demand-side measures that cut consumption and supply-side measures that limit production. Alternatives include switching to electricity, green hydrogen and biofuel. Most premature deaths from air pollution are due to fossil fuels, and the health benefits of phase-out, valued in money, exceed the cost of the 2 °C goal. Governments still subsidized fossil fuels by about $500 billion a year as of 2019, and the IMF's wider definition gave $5.2 trillion in 2017. As of 2024, global fossil fuel use was still rising, as it has since 1965. Workers and politicians tied to fossil industries tend to oppose phase-out unless they have strong alternatives.

nature-clim-203.title: Counting emissions where made or where consumed
nature-clim-203.text: In Norway, 69% of CO2 comes from making goods for export. Under production-based accounting, such a country could meet its targets just by exporting less. There are two main ways to count a nation's emissions. Production-based accounting counts emissions made on its territory, including exports but excluding imports. Consumption-based accounting counts those caused by what it consumes, imports included. Policy favors the production method because it is easier to measure, but it misses the emissions in traded goods. The consumption method traces products through global supply chains with multi-regional input-output models. It is more uncertain, needs more data and depends on international cooperation. The literature disagrees which method is fairer and better for policy, and some propose sharing responsibility.

nature-clim-221.title: The emissions gap: pledges versus need
nature-clim-221.text: Each year, UNEP's Emissions Gap Report measures the difference between the cuts countries pledge and the cuts needed to meet a temperature goal. UNEP first assessed the gap in November 2010, against the pledges of {{ref:nature-clim-061}} and a likely chance of meeting 2 °C. The 2020 report said 1.5 °C needs a 57% global cut from 2019 levels by 2030. In 2022 it said emissions needed to be almost halved. The 2024 report found current policies would likely lead to 3.1 °C of warming, and full pledges to 1.9 °C.

nature-clim-138.title: Carbon dioxide removal: taking CO2 back out of the air
nature-clim-138.text: As of 2023, about 2 gigatons of CO2 a year were removed from the air, almost all by planting forests. That equals 4% of yearly human greenhouse gas emissions. Carbon dioxide removal is deliberate human activity that takes CO2 out of the air and stores it durably on land, underground, in the ocean or in products. It is also called carbon removal, greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions. Net zero needs deep emission cuts first, then removal as well. Removal counterbalances emissions that are hard to eliminate, such as some from farming and aviation. Methods include afforestation, reforestation, carbon farming, burning plants for energy while storing the CO2, and machines that pull CO2 from the air for storage. They can be grouped by their place in the carbon cycle or by how long they store carbon, from decades to thousands of years. A 2019 NASEM report estimated that current safe and economic methods could remove up to 10 gigatons a year if fully deployed. Removal differs from carbon capture and storage at a power plant, which cuts new emissions but does not lower the CO2 already in the air.

nature-clim-199.title: Geoengineering: deliberately reshaping the climate
nature-clim-199.text: Geoengineering, or climate engineering, is deliberate large-scale intervention in Earth's climate system to counteract human-caused climate change. It usually covers two categories. Large-scale carbon dioxide removal is generally counted as mitigation. The other, {{ref:nature-clim-211}}, reflects some sunlight back to space. The two differ greatly in mechanisms, timelines and risks, and are now usually discussed separately. A common objection is that focusing on these technologies could undermine efforts to cut emissions. Effective governance and international oversight are widely seen as essential.

nature-clim-201.title: Who governs geoengineering?
nature-clim-201.text: No single treaty governs geoengineering. The rules are mostly specific to each method. In 2010 the treaty described in {{ref:nature-gov-015}} set a non-binding framework requiring scientific justification, environmental assessment and oversight. A 2013 amendment to the London Protocol created a binding framework for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization. It has not entered into force.

nature-clim-167.title: The energy transition: leaving fossil fuels behind
nature-clim-167.text: Energy production and use cause most human greenhouse gas emissions, and fossil fuels still meet over three-quarters of energy needs. An energy transition is a major structural change in how energy is supplied and used. Today it means the shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy. The current transition aims to cut energy emissions mainly by phasing down fossil fuels and running as much as possible on low-carbon electricity. It is not the first. During the Industrial Revolution, societies moved from wood and biomass to coal, then to oil and gas. The term itself arose after the 1973 oil crisis, and Jimmy Carter popularized it in 1977. Since the late 2010s, falling solar and wind costs have driven the change. Yet progress is slow. Despite decades of climate policy, transitions have not sped up beyond historical trends, and they remain off track for agreed warming goals.

nature-clim-172.title: Energy justice: who gains and who pays
nature-clim-172.text: Cities often gain from energy systems while rural areas bear the burdens. Energy justice aims for communities to gain affordable, safe and sustainable energy and to take part in decisions about it. It seeks to share benefits and burdens fairly across social groups, regions and generations. Its three main tenets are distributive justice, recognition justice and fair process. Distributive justice concerns how revenues, infrastructure sites and costs are shared. Recognition justice asks who is ignored. Fair process, explored in {{ref:nature-gov-220}}, requires transparent decisions and meaningful consultation. Some scholars add restorative and cosmopolitan justice to capture international inequalities and harms from fossil fuels. The energy justice cycle follows the system from extraction through production, supply and consumption to decommissioning and waste. The stakes are real, because transitions may worsen energy insecurity for low-income households.

nature-clim-190.title: Coal phase-out
nature-clim-190.text: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel. The IEA estimates it caused over 30% of warming above pre-industrial levels. Coal power emits about a tonne of CO2 per megawatt hour, twice as much as gas. Stopping coal burning in power plants and elsewhere is therefore central to the fossil fuel phase-out. Its health and environmental benefits exceed its costs, by over 1% of GDP a year according to one estimate. The IEA's 1.5°C pathway would require closing around 70% of existing coal capacity early. Germany uses reverse auctions to pay coal plants to close early, and some countries retire coal miners early. Economists have suggested a Coasean bargain, in which developed countries help pay for developing countries' phase-out. In 2021 the pact described in {{ref:nature-clim-087}} agreed to a coal phase-down.
